utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the next witness there will be no protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me? It seems not. Good afternoon, Witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. You may sit down, please. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear the translation into B/C/S, I'm sorry, I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can we lower the ELMO, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You won't forget, Mr. Krsnik, to ask him to tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bender?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I know there is your first time here, maybe even in your entire life that you are in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, I am for the first time in such a situation. I am very happy to be -- I'm glad to be here and I hope I'll manage to find my bearings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to give you just the basic instructions for a better cooperation and for the better work and so that we can actually go quickly through the subject that is we have envisaged for today's examination. In front of you, there is a transcript on the screen.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you see the cursor that is moving? Since we are speaking the same language, when the cursor stops, as it has just stopped now, then I am going to ask you to start giving your answer.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: There is no need to rush. Please take your time, the transcript is a very important thing so the translation is very important, and the interpreters really have a very hard job, they have to translate, convey the message, not only the words. So let's start -- can you please first introduce yourself to the Honours? First your first name, the last name and then your short curriculum vitae until 1990 and then after that, very briefly, all the offices that you held after 1990 and we will talk about the subjects later on. So a few sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I am Ivan Bender. I was born 3rd, January, 1947. My father was Mate, my mother was Andica. I was born in Zelenikovac, in Neum municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I finished primary school in my native village in the general area of Hutovo, then I finished classical grammar school in Capljina and then after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Then I finished the academy for education in Mostar. I have a degree in mathematics and physics. That was in the 1967, and in 1986, I graduated from the law school in Mostar. At the beginning of my career, I worked as a mathematics teacher, a teacher of mathematics and physics and then I was the principal of an elementary school. After that, I was the President of the municipal conference of the Socialist Alliance in Neum and I held two mandates, two, one-year mandates. After that, I was director of the branch office of the business bank in Neum, with the first multi-party elections in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the first multi-party elections, I was elected as the President of the municipal assembly of Neum. That was in November of 1990. After that, for several years, effectively until 1998, I held responsible offices in Neum municipality. It is important to say that in the first multi-party elections, I was elected with almost 100 per cent majority into the municipal council as the representative of the municipal assembly of Neum, so I was elected into the municipal council of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I remained there for as long as this municipal council existed, and functioned. After that, after the Washington and Dayton agreements and the establishment of the Constituent Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I continued my mandate as a representative in the constituent assembly. After the war, after the elections, I was elected into the assembly of the county of Herzegovina and Neretva, and at the same time, I was elected as a representative in the House of Peoples of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian Parliament. I would like to point out that during that -- in that period, I also held the post of the President of the Group of Croatian Representatives in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so these were the most important things, and if there is anything else you would like to know, please ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Something about the period between 1990 and what we are interested in, we will come to that in a certain order. So I shall come back to that period. Just briefly, did you held any offices in the HZ HB or HR HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, I held most responsible offices in the legislative bodies, both of HZ HB and HR HB. So the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us just briefly what offices were those, just to inform the Trial Chamber about the facts of your activities at the beginning and later on, we will go into details?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Upon the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna -- upon the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I was a member of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. After the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, for five or six months, I was the deputy president of the Chamber of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. After April, 1994, I was elected as a President of the Chamber of Representatives, which was the legislative body of the parliament of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and that lasted until the moment -- as long as the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me put the first question, Mr. Bender. Let's talk about your political world -- work. Can you describe your political work? Were you a member of any political party? We are talking about the period starting with the year 1990.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: At the beginning I would like to point out that until 1990, for ten years, I was a member of the League of Communists of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia until 1989. With the beginning of multi-party system in our area, I joined the committee for the establishment of the Croatian Democratic Union for Neum municipality, and I was elected as the first president of the municipal committee of the Croatian Democratic Union in Neum, and I was its president in several mandates. At the same time, I would like to point out that I was also elected to the -- to hold most responsible offices in the Croatian Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina but we can go into detail on that -- this much for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us where Neum is and then during the examination I'm going to give you the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that Their Honours actually get an insight into the geographical position of Neum.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: For your information, I would like to say that Neum is the only municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina which has exit [as interpreted] to the Adriatic Sea. If you have a map in front of you, you would find it difficult to locate it because it is the only municipality in the south of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What is your -- after the establishment of HZ HB what was your position and did you have a role at the state level after the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, I became the -- a member of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. At the same time, at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was a representative in the Council of Municipalities in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Chamber of Municipalities in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did -- when was your mandate discontinued, why? And in what year? So your mandates, can you tell us something about HZ HB, the Washington period, the Dayton period, the post-Dayton period, so can you tell us something about that? When was your mandate discontinued and why?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I am going to gladly answer this question but it will take sometime because I have to answer all the questions that you have just put me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just, if you could just tell us whether your mandate was discontinued and what year and why? Because we will come back to that. I just want an introduction into this general question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: So, I suppose we will clarify all of my functions and offices during the examination, because I already said that I held several offices in Neum in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on, in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is important, what I would like to point out at the moment is that my mandate in the legislative bodies of the -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina was discontinued in 1998. As a lawyer by profession, I must say that this was done in an illegal and illegitimate way by the high commissioner and some bodies at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was removed from the list for the assembly of the county -- of the county of Neretva and Herzegovina before the elections in 1998, not because of my own mistakes and failures, but as was written because the Croatian television, you understand the Croatian television from Zagreb, from another state, in one of its programmes -- in one of its programmes, promoted the Croatian HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and based on that, as a result of that, I could no longer hold an office in the legislative body, although I was not responsible, but somebody, it was somebody who took the right to do it on my behalf. So, if Your Honours are interested in that, I can submit all the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So this was an unilateral decision of the high commissioner for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes. Some bodies in the office of the high commissioner, not himself personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can the high representative replace in the same way judges, those who win in the elections? Who has given him the right to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Formally and legally, he shouldn't do that, and he shouldn't be allowed to do that. But somebody gave him the power, or he gave himself the power to replace both the judges and the prosecutors, to remove the people on the list, remove members of the Presidency, all sorts of things that have nothing whatsoever to do with common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I would like to clarify just one thing. You mentioned the word "federation." Can you say to this Court when was Bosnia and Herzegovina, when did Bosnia and Herzegovina stop being a republic and what did it consist of? You've mentioned the word "federation." When did Bosnia and Herzegovina, by what document, stop being a republic and what did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina as a republic functioned until the multi-party elections and after that, but effectively after the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and by the -- when the Serbs actually left Bosnia and Herzegovina and its institutions of government, Bosnia and Herzegovina continued to function as a republic, but with two peoples, because one people left. All the republican structures. The Washington Agreement served to establish the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and after that, we cannot talk about the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Has -- was this formalised by the Dayton agreement and what is the name of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The talks about the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina continued in Dayton, and as it was written in all the Dayton documents, there is no Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is Bosnia and Herzegovina without the republic, the word "republic" unfortunately, some representatives and some bodies have continued to abuse the name "republic." Although Your Honours, I have to repeat that after the Dayton agreement, what exists is Bosnia and Herzegovina without the addition of "republic" and its organisation will be determined by the peoples residing in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And just briefly, how is Bosnia and Herzegovina divided and how has it lived since 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: We -- it makes us angry when people say "Bosna." Bosnia and Herzegovina lives and functions and please let us not aggravate the witness by saying just "Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Since Dayton, since 1995, Bosnia and Herzegovina has been divided into two parts. It has been divided into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, mostly inhabited by Croats and Muslims, who will later on call themselves Bosniaks. The other part of Bosnia and Herzegovina is Republika Srpska. Imagine the name [as interpreted], Republika Srpska, which actually accounts for 49 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All the -- according to the 1991 census, Serbs were -- accounted for only 30 per cent of the total population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have to emphasise and I have to repeat, that Croats accounted for 17.5 per cent of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that Muslims, i.e. Bosniaks, accounted for some 44 per cent of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that pursuant to the Dayton Accord, they now have only 51 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this has been internationally recognised?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes. It has been recognised as such. I don't believe it is fair, it is just, it is not a solution that will satisfy Croats, Muslims or Serbs at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You owe me another answer. How -- did you stop engaging in politics in 1989? What was the sanction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I was removed from the list and I cannot hold any legislative or executive posts in the state structures of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you've been denied your civil rights?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Why, of course, because if one may not be elected and represent his people, then it means that that man has been denied his civil rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very good. And let me ask you the last introductory question. Was the HZ HB throughout 1993 and in 1994, were you there when it acted?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: We, on the basis of our estimates and our decisions, we decided to freeze the work of the HZ HB at that time because we thought that under wartime conditions, our Croat Democratic Union should not function. So it froze its activity temporarily, but it did not cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For the interpretation the transcript says, I asked you about the Croat Democratic Union and the transcript says HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: No, I have to make a correction. I'm referring to the freezing of the activity of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you, but very briefly, we are now moving to those things which the Defence believes that your knowledge could be very useful for the Defence. So the first question: When was the HDZ formed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was the platform of the party that you belonged to? But very briefly, because the Chamber has already heard a great deal from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The preparations for the establishment of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina started sometime in late 1989 and early 1990. The convention of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina was organised in August, 1990, and at that time, we also elected a leadership of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, if you wish to know more, I can go into details or about presidents of the Croat Democratic Union or rather about the composition of its leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But generally speaking, what was your programme, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: As regards the programme of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is common knowledge, because it was written very clearly, because the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the public at large have been informed about it. According to our -- in our programme we first say what was our view of the former state of Yugoslavia, and we said that we saw it as a community that is a confederation of republics. Unfortunately, it did not come true and you know what kind of war was waged down there, and we can talk about that later. And as for Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, we saw it as a decentralised multi-ethnic Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about its organisation, what did the programme say about the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: We said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: It should be a decentralised community of three peoples, Croats, Serbs and Muslims, who later on came to be called Bosniaks, and we would discuss and agree on its organisation, because there were different proposals and a number of initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did you -- did you intend to operationalise it by military means?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: No. We could not do that. How could we? Since we had no army. We were planning to do it politically, using democratic means, conducting talks and in agreement with the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did you at that time submit any reports on the work of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the HDZ of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: We never submitted reports on the work of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the HDZ in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. And did the programme of the HDZ of BH, was it defined? Was it written down by the HDZ of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Well, we get very angry when we hear questions like that, because we think that in the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had all the bodies, we had our leadership, we had our programmes, we adopted whatever decisions were necessary, and we reported to and accounted to only our people, that is the membership of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the question of the internal organisation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what about, according to the HDZ programme, was it specified and who did that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: All the programmes, all the decisions of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina were taken by us in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, it was our bodies who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Bender, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal alleges that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina had in its programme, included in its programme, a plan to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina and create areas jointly with Croatia, within the boundaries, says the Prosecutor, of the banovina. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: No, that is not true and it is not correct. All our acts, all our documents, clearly speak of Bosnia and Herzegovina and our future in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our subsequent Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, that is Croat Republic Herceg-Bosna, is part and parcel of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, I will now show you Prosecutor's Exhibit P899. You are a teacher. Are you familiar with this map from the past?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. During my education, I learned about the plans of the Banovina Hrvatska, but it had nothing to do with the plans of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, very well. That is not what I had in mind. Not right now. What I wanted to ask you was when was Yugoslavia divided like this? Do you know that? And what was this division of Yugoslavia, subdivision of Yugoslavia called? How long was it in force?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Well, that was during World War II, sometime it was done sometime in 1939, 1940, and those were plans of some other people, of some other generations, not those that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know if there were republics or banovinas at the time, I mean in the territory of the then kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I know that there were banovinas, no republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know what was the name of the banovina which is light red, which is coloured light red?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I think it was called Vrbas Banovina but I'm not quite sure because I can't see it all that well, with its seat in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you now please be so kind as to take the pointer, will you show the -- Their Honours where Neum is? Perhaps this is a good opportunity to do that. On the map. If you need glasses, please do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes. I shall be happy to. Neum is here on the map, and it says here, so it's quite near the Neretva, on the Adriatic coast, in this gulf here, as I am pointing, and it is the only Bosnia-Herzegovinian municipality with an outlet to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now I will show you another map, which is marked P3.4. The Prosecutor alleges that the HZ HB overlaps with this banovina. Will you compare the two maps and tell us if that allegation is true and which are these areas, and may I warn you, the yellow line is the border of the HZ HB as affirmed by the Prosecutor. These are maps made by the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: As a founding father or one of the founding fathers of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, I must say that what is marked here in yellow is not the territory which was part of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you take the pointer and explain what was part of HZ HB and which wasn't, which were the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: If we start from the south, municipality of Neum was part and is part of the Croat community and Croat Republic Herceg-Bosna. Likewise, Capljina, Citluk, Ljubuski, Listica, that is Siroki Brijeg, then Grude, Posusje, Duvno, which says, that is what it says here, but it is Tomislavgrad. Then Livno, Prozor, that is Rama, also part of the municipality of Trebinje inhabited most mostly by Croats. The municipality of Ravno, which is this area that I'm pointing at. It also belongs to the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna. Then the major part of the Stolac municipality inhabited by Croats mostly and some Bosniaks. It is also part of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just a moment. Since we are talking about Stolac, the Prosecutor alleges that the majority of the population there are Muslims, that is Bosniaks. So, how could it then become part of the HZ HB? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I shall be happy to do that, because it depends on which census you take into account. Under the 1991 census in the territory of the whole municipality of Stolac, the Muslims were the majority, accounting for some 44 per cent. There were some 33, 34 per cent of Croats. And the rest were Serbs. However, the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna -- into the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna was integrated that part of the Stolac municipality where the Croats had the majority, not the whole of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you mean that the HZ HB incorporated parts of municipalities rather than entire territories of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: That's right, parts of the municipalities of Stolac and I've already said part of the municipality of Trebinje. Then parts of some other municipalities in central Bosnia and we can talk about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this -- the part around the Sava River, did it also become part of the HZ HB? I don't see it here in the map.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The municipalities of Odzak, Bosanski Samac, Orasje, Bosanski Brod, parts of the municipalities of Brcko, Modrica and Derventa were also part of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna. It is important to explain that the municipality of Zepce is incorporated in the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna and here a number of municipalities here are not part of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna. For instance Fojnica, then the major part of the municipality of Travnik, and as for the municipality of Skender Vakuf, only a part of it, the municipality of Dobratici which was recognised later on and which exist in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina too. And to sum it up, what is in yellow here is not a true boundary of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna because it encompasses territories which are not parts of the Herceg-Bosna and it excludes some municipalities which are part of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna. And I need to repeat the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna and this territory here have nothing to do with the Banovina Hrvatska. If you compare these two maps, you can see it for yourselves very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Let us leave those maps aside. Tell me, please, can you bring the ELMO down? The Prosecution also alleges that the Republic of Croatia took decisions for the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also laid down the policy of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: No, that is not true. And I wish to tell you and the Prosecutor and Their Honours to say, I want to wish to tell them very clearly that in the Croat community -- in the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had all the necessary organs. We took our decisions independently, and our programmes too. And what is very important, we are neither under aged nor are we half-witted. We are an organised community of intellectuals, of capable people, of people perfectly up to deciding on their own fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now who could be the member -- who could become a member of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Their Honours and the Prosecutor and you personally can easily see it from our documents. You can easily see who could become a member of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but let me clarify this. One -- a member of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina could be any person of age, embracing the -- adhering to the programme, to the statute of the party and signing the application form. In confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbs in the ranks of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes. True, not a large number of Serbs who were members of the Croat Democratic Union. And as for the Muslims, there were quite a number of them who were members of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had on our, in our Presidency, that is the supreme body of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were also two Muslims. One was vice-president and another was a member of the Presidency. These are Habid Hodzic and Nusret Sisic and a number of them were members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to repeat those two names very slowly so that the interpreters can interpret them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Could I also see the text on the screen again because I've lot the transcript and I cannot follow. The vice-president of the Croat Democratic Union, that is one of the vice-presidents, was a Muslim Habid Hodzic from Sarajevo. A member of the Presidency was Nusret Sisic, I also think he comes from somewhere around Sarajevo but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, did the HDZ, that is HZ HB later on, as an association of all the parties with -- well, I'll put it this way -- with the Croat prefix, did they all aspire to an ethnically pure territory or perhaps did the programme say so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object to the leading on these kinds of questions. He can ask what the programme is but I let it pass up until now but we are having continuously leading questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly a leading question, Mr. Krsnik. You have to pose your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't say that I asked many leading questions. That is what my learned friend thinks, but let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'll ask you this: The Prosecutor alleges that the HZ HB, that is the HDZ, wanted an ethnically pure territory in Herzegovina so that it could annex it to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I don't think that corrects the problem. I also object to this form of putting to the witness what the Prosecution alleges. I think it's an improper form of questioning. Counsel can ask open-ended fact questions. "What was the programme at the relevant time of the party?" But the question just put in fact, I think respectfully, is worse than the former question. It's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honours. I thought that it would be better to move faster. We all know what the Prosecutor is out to establish. I thought it was simply speed matters up. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what the Prosecution said before, just rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. I thought it would be much easier but as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In 1990, 1991, then in 1992, 1992, and then in 1993, the programme of the HDZ, HZ HB, HR HB, briefly, did the objectives laid down in the programmes of these bodies reflect an aspiration to acquire territory which would be taken out from Bosnia-Herzegovina, a wish or a reality, to take out something from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really don't know how to word it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... same question in many different ways. What we want you to do is pose a different question. What I might suggest to you what you might ask if it's convenient for you and if accords with your plan, if you might ask this witness first to tell us briefly what the HDZ platform was in 1989-90, did it change, as you develop, and then ask us what the platform of the HZ HB was. But ask them in different questions, not all rolled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I always accept your suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, you've heard, Mr. Bender, so let us move on to the first question. So the HDZ platform, did it change over time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: From the foundation of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we've had our programmes, our platforms and our documents, and never, not a single body, not a single act, not a single document, did we ever mention any ethnically pure lands in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about the HZ HB platform and did it change with time? Likewise?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: From the outset, from its inception, from the foundation of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, and later on, during the period of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we had our documents, our plans, our platforms, which were based on the programme of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They did not change, but they were developed, they were improved, they were amended but the basic concept remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, then what was the political solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we look at the HDZ views, let's say from the beginning of 1992 onward?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Your Honours, and the others present here probably know that as for the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were several plans. The Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina accepted all these plans because we expected a peaceful solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unfortunately, others did not want the same and to be more specific, those were Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me for the interruption. I did not have in mind the international peace talks, just the position of HDZ on Bosnia-Herzegovina starting with 1992 onwards. What was the position of HDZ with regard to the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I told you at the beginning, and I'm going to repeat it, that HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in its platforms, outlined and wrote that -- that it wanted a decentralised, multi-ethnic Bosnia and Herzegovina, a community of three constitutive and sovereign people, Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks. And as for the specific organisation, we will talk about it, we will agree, at the competent bodies, the competent bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina will agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did -- were these positions confirmed by the Croatian people and if they were, when was it and by what act?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: All of our acts that were passed by us confirmed this and most specifically by the preparations and by the organisation of the referendum on 29 February and 1st March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, forgive me for interrupting, could you ask your witness if the platform of the HDZ at the beginning, which wanted a decentralised country with three constitutive and sovereign people, sorry, was it intended that they would live in a multi-ethnic society or when he talks about constitutive and sovereign peoples were they to be separated? Isn't that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, I believe you've heard the question. Could you please reply?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I will gladly do that. I said, and I will repeat, and I will prove that by an example, I'm going to show you how we saw Bosnia-Herzegovina and what solutions we sought for Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to our platform and according to our wishes and proposals, Bosnia-Herzegovina was -- we saw it as a decentralised Bosnia and Herzegovina, but a community, multi-ethnical community of three peoples living side by side, together. Let me just clarify that on an example. If a father has a farm and three sons, during his life it will be good if the father agrees with his sons, where each of them will live and how. So to give each of his sons a part of the farm that will belong to him. And if the father doesn't do that, the father being an authority in this case, it is certain that the lives of the three sons will not be good because they will quarrel with each other. But if the father says exactly what belongs to each of the -- his sons, they will be able to live together as good friends and real, genuine brothers, without any arguments, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Maybe this is a difference in the two languages. You said side by side, together. What is the meaning of multi-ethnic? Is it together mixed in one village or one city? Can you explain the notion of multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Obviously I said in my -- at the beginning of -- we are talking about multi-ethnic Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be composed in the following way: Where there is a majority of Serbs, a majority of Croats, and a majority of Muslims, and in between there will be the three peoples living together. Let me try and avoid any ambiguity. So, wherever Croats make a majority, there will also be Muslims and Bosniaks and Serbs likewise, in the areas where Serbs are a majority, and the same goes for the areas where Bosniaks account for a majority, and all of them will enjoy the same rights, the same civil rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We stopped at the referendum. That was the last thing we said. Why referendum? Who was it who imposed the referendum? Do you know? And what was the result of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Their Honours and all the other present probably know what happened at the end of the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s, in the area of the former Eastern Bloc. The Soviet Union collapsed. The Berlin Wall fell. The former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia could no longer exist in its previous form. The Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia gained their independence. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, we started thinking about how to proceed, how to go on. Obviously, we had to reach an agreement, an agreement between Croats, Serbs and Muslims, i.e. Bosniaks, about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the republican parliament, that is the Chamber of Municipalities and the Chamber of Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we discussed this issue on several occasions. And more specifically at a session on 24, 25 and 26 January, 1992, we discussed the issue of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we defined the question that we would put to the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We wanted to ask them where they saw Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they saw Bosnia-Herzegovina in -- as part of the Republic of Yugoslavia without Slovenia and Croatia, or whether they saw it as an independent state. Croats said very clearly that they wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state. The same position was given by Muslims. And Serbs wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to be part of Yugoslavia at all costs. The referendum on the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina was organised on the 29th February and 1st of March, 1992. The participants in the referendum were only Croats and Muslims, whereas the Serbs boycotted the referendum so they did not vote in the referendum. The turnout of Croats and the response was over 90 per cent, I think it was 98 per cent of Croats voted in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state, whereas Muslims played a bit of a tactical game, I would say, because over 60 -- what over 60 per cent of Muslims voted for Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, you still owe me an answer to the question whether this referendum was imposed by somebody, whether somebody said that the referendum had to take place.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Who would it be to actually impose that? Who would actually impose this issue to be discussed? I said very clearly that in -- at the parliament of our republic, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think we understood each other. There has been a misunderstanding. If the referendum had not taken place, would Bosnia and Herzegovina have become an independent state, without this referendum? Do you know anything about Badinter Commission?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Of course, I know everything about that commission. I know exactly what it did. If the referendum had not taken place and if the response had not been the way it was, Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain -- would have remained a part of Yugoslavia. You can see from the turnout and the response given at the referendum that Croats actually deserve most credit for the independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Without Croats, Bosnia and Herzegovina would not exist as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the "Livno Issue," and what is the connection of this issue with the referendum?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I said that in the parliament of our republic, we defined the question that would be put at the referendum, and this question was submitted to parliamentary parties for their consideration and for them to prepare the referendum. The Croatian Democratic Union, at its meeting held in Livno at the beginning of February, considered the proposal for the question to be put at the referendum, and defined its counterproposal which differed somewhat from the proposal defined at the assembly of the republic. And it submitted this counterproposal to the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina for their consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please tell me, did you have a list of members of HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know who its members were? I'm asking this just -- let me rephrase the question. Was Mladen Naletilic, who is my client, was he a member of HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Their Honours probably know that every serious party has a membership list, a list of members that belong to this party. At that time, I was a vice-president of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I -- I could access all the documents. I also could access a list of members of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your client, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, has never been a member of HDZ, i.e. he was not on our list, so he's not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him at any of your meetings, either of HDZ or HZ HB or HR HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I have not seen your client in any of the bodies of HDZ, HZ HB, HR HB. So personally I have never seen Mr. Mladen Naletilic in any of these meetings of any of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me go back to the "Livno Issue." I wanted to actually bring each subject to an end. That's why I asked you about my client. Have you ever received an answer, i.e. have you received the answer to the counterproposal put forth by HDZ to the republican body? Have you ever received the answer from that body? Was your proposal accepted or not, and who was it who decided whether it would be accepted or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I said that at our meeting in Livno, the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina defined its proposal of the question to be put at the referendum, which differed somewhat from the proposal defined at the end of January at the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We never received an answer to our proposal, i.e. to our letter, but at that time, the leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we decided that despite the fact that we did not fully agree with the question to be put at the referendum, that we will still invite the Croatian people to come to the referendum and to vote for an independent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And finally, what was the difference between the proposal, between the question that was finally put at the referendum and the proposal of the Croatian Democratic Union? So what was the difference?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I do not have the exact wording of the question that we defined in Livno, but I did have it, and I still have it at home. So, the Croatian Democratic Union wanted to put the question in addition to the question about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as per our proposal, the proposal of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we also wanted to raise the issue of the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina once it gained its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, did anybody opt for an Unitarian solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina? If yes, who was it and what would such an organisation meant for Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: At that time, what -- one could tell from the platform and the appearances of Muslim representatives, one could tell, and one could conclude, that they wanted a centralised civil Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was not convenient, which Croats did not find convenient at all, because Croats are the least numerous people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if Bosnia and Herzegovina was not organised in the way proposed by us, if it was a centralised state of a civil type, based on the principle "one person, one vote" in its entire territory, Croats would always lose in every election. So we wanted that the total number of Croats accounted for one vote as the total number of Bosniaks and that the two peoples agreed on the organisation of their state to the mutual satisfaction of both Croats and Muslims. So the same would be -- for example this would be the case if the Netherlands and Germany would make one state and each people would have one vote, and we know what the ratio of the respective populations are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let us move on to HZ HB and HR HB. What were the reasons for the inception of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The reasons for the inception of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were -- there were several reasons, and some of them, the most important reasons, were defined in our document on the constitution of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, do you mind if I ask you a question now instead of the end, because when it's at the end sometimes we are very caught for time and so on. If I'm to follow your political thesis, you wanted a Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be made up of three constituent and equal peoples, but that each -- each of the areas which made up Bosnia and Herzegovina were to be determined by the majority ethnic group. So the Serbs would be in the area where they dominated, which is the north and east of the country, the Croats would be in a separate area in the southwest of the country and the Bosniaks would be in the middle. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree with that, because we did not want a Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What did you want then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina organised on the principle, on the same principles as Belgium, as Switzerland, and you can see that it functions well, both in Belgium and in Switzerland. We wanted cantonal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And the cantons would be determined according to the ethnic groups, isn't that right, the majority groups would form certain cantons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would not be a condition. We said, and we wrote down that we wanted multi-ethnical counties, i.e. cantons, but obviously with the majority population, because that's the way the population is composed in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, what naturally follows from there, and what logically follows is that when a canton is formed to accommodate the dominant ethnic group, the situation forever more will be that the other two ethnic groups will never win a majority in an election, just exactly what you were objecting to in relation to the former republic. I want to you think about that, because it's time for a break. And maybe you can convince me that my empirical deductions are false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's time for a break. We will resume at 5.30. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, are you ready to answer Judge -- Judge Clark's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am quite ready to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that Her Honour will agree with me when I say that Switzerland and Belgium are well organised states which come across no problems in their functioning. If we organise Bosnia-Herzegovina along those same principles, then at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we shall be -- we shall be organising those bodies and those institutions which a state needs. However, the composition of those bodies must be -- of course, multi-ethnic, Croats, Serbs and Muslims who rotate and who take decisions by consensus. No, not by majority of votes. All that is not related to the state takes place in counties, that is cantons, which are again multi-ethnic, but with a majority Croats or Muslims, that is Bosniak, population, and it can be -- it lends itself to good organisation and good consultations and everything can work in good order. We in the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we also had another proposal for Bosnia-Herzegovina and its structuring. And that was an union of three republics, of a Croat republic, Muslim republic and Serb republic, and it could also be organised, I'm sure, very well and it will function smoothly. But I need to point out that the current organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is not the best because some peoples are privileged. I wonder why can the Serbs have and must -- and why must they have their own state, Republika Srpska, and the Croats cannot and are not supposed to. In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are chiefly Croats and Bosniaks, and unless we decentralise the federation, made of parts which we call counties, and the ratio in the federation is about one to six, that is one Croat to six Muslims, that is Bosniaks, and if we adopt the principle "one man, one vote," then the Croats will never have their representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: But Mr. Bender, didn't -- in the first multi-party elections, didn't the Croats have a very good representation in Sarajevo? Didn't they succeed in almost obtaining a majority relative to their numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had the Chamber of Peoples, which could prevent --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. Judge Clark was asking about the first elections, that was the elections in 1990, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I right, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: As for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation in 1990-91, the Croats were not protected, because the decisions were taken differently. They were taken in the Chamber of municipalities and the Chamber of citizens. That is there were no ethnic elements, Croats, Serbs and Muslims, and moreover, you could see that the Serbs wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to stay on in rump Yugoslavia and that the Muslims wanted a civil state where they could constitute a majority and take decisions in their own interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I take it, Mr. Bender, that there is no proportionate "PR" in your country? Proportionate representation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. There isn't. After Dayton, for a while, we had rather well-organised chambers of peoples of Croats and Bosniaks in the federation, which adopted all the crucial decisions or could prevent the adoption of wrong decisions, damaging decisions, but after the later decisions of the high representatives that I have already referred to, these chambers of peoples, that is Croats and Bosniaks, now have been organised in a different way, and I will take the liberty of informing Their Honours that the house in the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is to be made of 30 Croats and 30 Bosniaks, and a certain number of others, this Chamber now has only 14 Croats and some say that it is a sufficient quorum for the Chamber to take decisions, and I believe, Your Honour, that you know that 14 can never be a majority of 14, and it shouldn't take any decisions, yet, it does take such decisions. And now you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think Judge Diarra has some questions and also when I'm talking about PR, I'm not talking about representation in the parliament but how one votes, not one man one vote but that you have a choice and suppose you have ten candidates for one seat, that the electorate, the voter votes in order of his choice, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, so that the first -- it has to be more than one seater. So that if the first person has a surplus, his votes are divided it's the way it operates in Malta and Ireland, and it works very well for small parties, or else one party would always be in majority, it is a complicated and probably highly sophisticated democratic process. Might be a little difficult for a new country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krsnik, I am sorry that I am interrupting your examination-in-chief but this is very important for the continuation of the examination. The witness quoted the examples of Switzerland and Belgium, and this I'm afraid has led to a certain confusion because I do not think that Switzerland and Belgium function all that well, because of their administrative subdivision, it has to do with the principles governing life, that is the Swiss nationality is cultivated and the Belgian nationality is cultivated, the identity cards there does not say that somebody comes from -- that one is a German Swiss or something else and all the citizens vote for the best, for the most brilliant for the most efficient and the most honest nominee rather than, for instance, a Roman Swiss because of that. No, they do not vote for somebody because he comes from this or that part of Switzerland but because he's the best and because he can best address the problems of the society, where as in your case it is the difference which is cultivated. Before one becomes a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one is a Croat and that's what you're cultivating and when it comes to elected people, I think then one Croat then -- then it is that the Croat must always elect a Croat. That is what I believe that I have understood during your examination and I do not think that if we quote the examples of Switzerland and Belgium, we shall not be able to move ahead because we know how things function in those countries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Bosnia-Herzegovina can and should be organised along lines similar to Swiss or Belgian lines. I didn't say identically, but one needs to point out that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are three peoples. I repeat, three peoples, Croats, Serbs and Bosniaks. And that Bosnia-Herzegovina needs to be organised as a state so as to keep all the three peoples satisfied. Otherwise, the prospects of Bosnia-Herzegovina are not good, but I hope you will agree with me that the Croat will always trust most Croats, a Serb will always trust a Serb best, and a Bosniak will always place his greatest trust in a Bosniak, even though at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have a Presidency made of Croats, a Serb and Bosniaks, who talk amongst themselves and always take decisions by consensus, of all the three. They rotate as the Presidents of that body, and you can see how it can function well. But if we allowed two to outvote a third one, then there is no future in that. What happened last time in the elections of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what happened is that a Serb and a Bosniak elected a Croat as the Prime Minister, the President of the Council of Ministers, bypassing the will of the Croats. Now, gentlemen, think for yourselves. Is it the future? Are these the prospects? Does this lead to the solution of the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean against the will of the Croat constituency?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, because the Croats were prevented from electing their own representative. Specifically, I can clarify this. The Croat people proposed Martin Raguz as the President of the council of ministers, that is the Prime Minister. The Serbs and the Bosniaks did not go along with that nomination. They nominated therefore, that is the Serb and the Bosniak proposed Bozo Matic, a Croat, to the post of the Prime Minister. Now, gentlemen, may a Serb and a Bosniak elect a Croat who will be representing Croats? I do not think that it can be so anywhere in the civilised world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now that you've started the discussion, I must say that my concept was slightly different, but Her Honour, Judge Diarra now encouraged me to ask. What were the plans of the international community? Were they identical with these proposals? Could you explain Cutilheiro, Vance-Owen, or Owen-Stoltenberg's plan, but briefly, if you're familiar with them? What did they propose?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: International community had many proposals and solutions for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Cutilheiro's plan was good and the Croats accepted it. Also the Vance-Owen and Owen-Stoltenberg's plan, the Croats accepted them. But unfortunately, the Serbs did not. Likewise, representatives of the Muslims, that is Bosniaks, were playing tactical games and would say one thing today and two or three days later they would say something else, would sign or wouldn't sign, or rather would sign them today and tomorrow say that they had not signed them. We also had some proposals about provinces and at long last, this thing with first Washington and then Dayton happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me. Under the Cutilheiro's plan, but just in one sentence please, what was Bosnia to be divided?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I must correct you, don't ever mention Bosnia to me. Always say Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right because I corrected others. So I apologise, but, well, you know.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: This plan referred to the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an union of three republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The first plan, Cutilheiro's?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: It was the organisation of subdivision of Bosnia-Herzegovina into provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I've already said it. For a while in the beginning, there was an union of three republics, then again the Croats accepted all those plans but others failed to do that and so people continued to seek other solutions, and at long last, these solutions came up that were presented in Washington, that is Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then today, how has Bosnia been subdivided?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I need to say that Bosnia-Herzegovina was divided by another, not by the Croat people, and organised it asymmetrically in two parts, the Republika Srpska, with the predominant Serb population, and the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the predominant Bosniak and Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Now tell me, which were the main reasons for the establishment of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: To understand the reasons behind the establishment of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, we need to be familiar with the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and around Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. The Honourable Court and others who are present, I believe, know that the Serbs, Montenegrins and the so-called JNA started an open war with a view to conquering and subjugating first Slovenia and then Croatia. We in Bosnia and Herzegovina realised what was in store for us because we are the nearest to Serbia, that is Montenegro. We dare not just sit and wait for this aggressor to catch us unawares, to kill our wives, our children, and us if we are there unprepared. The map shows clearly the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbs, Montenegrins and the so-called JNA, in the war -- well, they attacked with all the resources available, East Croatia, that is Slavonia, in the north, then in the South Dubrovnik and the south of Croatia were also shelled from the territories and from all sides. The problems relative to Zadar, Knin and Karlovac are self-evident because the war threatened there and threatened to split Croatia into several parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, would you please answer the question in one sentence, please? If the Defence counsel needs more information, he will ask you the follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be brief. In two sentences. It is obvious that the war is being prepared because Bosnia and Herzegovina because the Serbs, Montenegrins and the JNA want to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina and keep it within rump Yugoslavia. The lawful representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina or specifically Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, at the time when the Serbs attack our inhabited place, Ravno, says, "This is not our war." But he's the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He even declares that he will invite the JNA to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what we, the Croats, had to do at a time like that, to create a body and get ready for the defence, and this was the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the position of citizens in the territory of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The citizens in the territory of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna enjoyed equal rights but also had equal duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of possible expulsion of people, of dismissal of people from their jobs or any discrimination against individuals based on racial, ethnic or any other grounds? What was the situation in schools? Namely we've heard here in this courtroom that there was discrimination, that people lost their jobs only because they were Muslims, for instance.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I feel I must deny such statements. Whoever may be making them. I repeat I am a member of the Presidency of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, as the legislative body, all citizens enjoyed the same rights and same duties. Many of them lost their jobs because the war is in the offing [as interpreted] and the war is starting. Some of the schools went on working and some didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just a point of clarification, the witness several times has testified, unless it's a translation issue which is one reason I'm asking, that he is -- he says, "I am a member of the Presidency of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna." Is he saying that in the present tense or is he saying he was in 1993? I think it's important to an understanding of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's a problem of translation. Mr. Krsnik, you may clarify this issue for us, asking some specific questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. If the witness says, "I was," then this is the past tense. And he keeps saying, "I was." And then it must be with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it must be clear. If I'm referring to the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna that is how it was at that time. Today, of course, the situation is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, was the HZ HB the product of your intentions? When I say "your" I mean the founding fathers of the HZ HB, to create a state within Bosnia-Herzegovina? First, who were the founders of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I believe that your -- Their Honours and all the others present here today have had the opportunity to see the decision on the foundation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. 30 legally elected representatives of municipalities from Bosnia-Herzegovina incepted the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was that contrary to the then constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the then --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I repeat, the situation was such that we had to organise ourselves in order to defend ourselves. We are talking about our lives, about defending our lives. The central organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina stopped functioning. The then president, Alija Izetbegovic, you heard his statements, and we, as the legally elected representatives of the Croatian people and others inhabiting the areas of these municipalities, i.e. other peoples, acted in that way in order to prepare ourselves to defend ourselves from Serbs, Montenegrins and the so-called JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You did not reply to my question. Was that in breach of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina when it comes to the defence of the state? I'm talking about the then constitution.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I repeat, at the time the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina had stopped functioning. Bosnia and Herzegovina should have acted on its duties and obligations and prepare itself for the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was the intention of the founders of the 30 municipalities to create a state within the state?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I already said, and I would like to repeat that, that we did not want to organise a state within the state. We wanted to organise a community that would be organised and that would defend itself from the aggressor that attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what money was used to incept HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: In the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, we had several currencies, we used several currencies. My people and me personally preferred a German mark, and that was the currency that we used the most, and in addition to the German mark, we also used American dollar, Croatian dinar, and then kuna -- Croatian kuna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, I believe the question asked by the Defence counsel is the source of those moneys. Where did you get those moneys to incept HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. The money for the Defence and for the normal functioning of life in the area of HZ HB was provided from our own sources down there. A lot of funds came from our people living abroad. So those who at the time lived in Europe, in the United States of America, and so on and so forth. And some of the money we also raised from our people living in the Republic of Croatia, so the immigrants living in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have your own bank so to say, a central or a state bank, central bank like every other country does?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: We have never had. We never had a central bank, a state bank, because we did not want the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and subsequently the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna be a state in the state, God forbid, an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So, you were saying that it was just a temporary form of organisation until the final agreement on the permanent organisation. I'm going to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You give the answer in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did HZ HB have a time of existence, a limited time of existence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, all our documents say that HZ HB and HR HB were just temporary organisations and that they will last for as long as we reach an agreement on the future organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Zagreb, when I say Zagreb I mean the Republic of Croatia, did the leadership of the Republic of Croatia dictate your decisions, the decisions that would be passed in the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat what I've already said. All the decisions in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna were taken and passed independently by our bodies, so nobody from the Republic of Croatia could influence or indeed did influence the decisions that we made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the beginnings of HVO? When was it incepted and what was its relationship with the HZ HB? Can you give us your views in order to help the Honourable Court clarify some of the issues?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I believe that the Honourable Court knows and if they don't know they should know, that the is HVO consists of two parts, two independent, separate parts. One is the Croatian Defence Council, as the military component, and the other is the Croatian Military Council, as the executive body of the government in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The decision on the establishment of the civilian part was made by the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the decision on the establishment of the military part, i.e. the army of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was made by our late president, Mr. Mate Boban. That was on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which body had the approximate status of a parliament, i.e. the legislature, in the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the legislative body was the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the executive part of the government was the Croatian Defence Council. The civilian part of the Croatian Defence Council. We are talking about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the things are different in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us what the differences were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Towards the end of August, 1993, when the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established, we had a president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we also had the Chamber of Representatives, and I was its president, while it functioned as the legislative part of the government, and we also had the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, as the executive part of the government, and we also organised the judiciary and it -- all of these were temporary bodies which was subsequently confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you personally know that the laws you passed, both in HZ HB and as well as in HR HB, that they received international confirmation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: All the laws and decisions that were made and passed by us were passed as temporary documents and because of the goal that I have already mentioned, during the functioning of both the HZ HB and HR HB, we did not ask for the international recognition of these institutions, but the international community, however tacitly, recognised them because it invited our representatives to the negotiations dealing with the future organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and after the Dayton agreement, the parliament of the federation passed a certain -- a piece of legislation whereby it confirmed all the decisions and acts that had been passed by the competent bodies of the HR HB and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Muslim -- as the Muslim part which had functioned at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The laws that you passed in HZ HB, HR HB, are they still in effect today?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: They are no longer in effect because after the Dayton agreement, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska were incepted and they now function based on the laws and other decisions which have been passed, but I repeat that the laws and all the other acts passed within the system of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and HR HB have been conferred by the competent bodies of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, who are the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Can you tell us, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Everybody knows, and I know it as well, as one of the leaders of HZ HB and HR HB, that the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are the Croatian Defence Council and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's what Muslims called their own Muslim armed forces, which has been confirmed in a number of meetings and by a number of documents. I believe that the Honourable Court is familiar with the Izetbegovic-Tudjman agreement which regulates these things in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which agreement are you referring to? Because we have seen a number of them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: That's the agreement on friendship and cooperation dating from July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We apologise on behalf of Mrs. Pinter, she did not hear because she does not have her headphones on. Yes. The Court is familiar with this agreement so I am not going to dwell upon it any longer. Do you personally know -- do you have any knowledge about the political views of Alija Izetbegovic? Have you had any contacts, personal contacts with him? What were his views of the entire situation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: During this -- all this time, we met in a number of meetings.
