I personally know, and I hope that the Honourable Court and all the other present here today also know, that Alija Izetbegovic, in 1983, was one of the founders of the Islam Declaration -- Islamic Declaration, which provided for the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the principles of an Islamic state, and it was exactly for this document that he had to serve a prison sentence in Foca. I know that he was there for a long time. The platform of the Party of Democratic Action officially promoted a civil Bosnia and Herzegovina, and secretly, what was being done was organising an Islamic state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have any personal meetings with him? Were you a member of the delegation in political negotiations? As for example the signing of various agreements, starting with this agreement on friendship and cooperation and others?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic and myself did not meet eyeball-to-eyeball, as one may say, but we were both members of some delegations, and we participated in negotiations, and as for this agreement dating from July, 1992, I did not participate in that particular meeting but I participated in a number of other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about the so-called negotiations in Graz, in Austria? Do you know what happened there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I know. I know because the representatives of the Croatian people who were there conveyed the message at the meetings of the competent bodies, I'm talking about Mr. Boras and Mr. Boban who told us that they -- that the discussion was about the future organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because they were supposed -- there should have been meetings between Boban and Karadzic, Boban and Izetbegovic and Boban and Karadzic or the three of them were supposed to meet all together, but as far as I know, and as I was informed from those who were there, Mr. Izetbegovic refused to meet Karadzic and that's why the negotiations fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that after this Graz meeting, that there was a meeting between the -- any Croatian delegation and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: There are even documents corroborating that fact that Izetbegovic and Boban did meet, and talked about cooperation and unfortunately, Mr. Izetbegovic said one thing and did the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And these negotiations were organised based on which international plan, do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I -- at the moment, I can't remember off my head [as interpreted]. There were a number of such plans and I don't know exactly which plan was the basis of this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you personally know -- are you familiar with a joint statement dating from April, 1993, issued by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the statement. I have that paper. And as far as I understand, both Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic signed this document and we would only be so lucky if this document has been followed through, because the situation today would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic denied ever having ever signed this document, and he has sent a letter to this effect to the Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Izetbegovic claims, but this wouldn't surprise me coming from him. My information, according to my information, both Mr. Izetbegovic -- Mr. Izetbegovic also signed this document, but Mr. Izetbegovic had been known to deny things that he has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we ask for the basis of this information we have absolutely no foundation for this except a bald assertion -- [Microphone not activated] basis for knowing Mr. Izetbegovic signed this [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours, I'm going to show the document to Mr. Bender and can I please ask Madam Registrar to help us with the document PP271? And can you please verify that this is a document that we have mentioned and give us the basis for your assertion? How do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: This witness has already told us that he didn't actually know what was being discussed, he doesn't remember. [Microphone not activated] What credibility can be attached to what he's going to say about Mr. Izetbegovic. [Microphone not activated] He's made it quite clear what he thinks about Mr. Izetbegovic so we can move on. It's not going to help us to prove anything. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept every intervention of yours, but I believe that there may have been a misunderstanding here because Mr. Bender, without seeing the document, he told us that he has personal knowledge about the things which were signed and now I have faced him with a document. He said that he did not know what plan was the basis of the negotiations between Boban-Karadzic, Boban-Izetbegovic. He said that he didn't know what plan was the basis of those negotiations but he didn't say about this document that he didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, [Microphone not activated] He said I don't know what Mr. Izetbegovic claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was to my question whether he knows. I don't know, I don't know whether it has been interpreted well. I haven't been following the translation. I said that Mr. Izetbegovic denied ever having signed this document by a letter to this Court. And then Mr. Bender says, "I don't know what Mr. Izetbegovic knows or doesn't know. I know what I know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did indeed say that I don't know what plan was the base of the negotiations, there were a number of such plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have to speak slowly because the translation is very important here so let's all speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I also said that I know that after the negotiations in Graz, that there were further talks which resulted in this joint statement. And we -- we were informed about this document at the meetings of our bodies in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna by Mr. Boban and Mr. Boras. I agree with this statement and I repeat we should only be so lucky if this statement has been followed through. It hasn't been followed through by the Muslim people, i.e. by its leader, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question is, "do you know whether Mr. Izetbegovic has signed this document or not?" From your personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because that -- we heard that from Mr. Boban and Mr. Boras that Mr. Izetbegovic had signed this document. Personally, I wasn't there, but we were told that by Mr. Boras and Mr. Boban. I hope that the Honourable Court has the document which corroborates this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, can you please tell me do you know how many inhabitants who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina live in the Republic of Croatia, how many people who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina live in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The exact number is not known but according to our estimates, the estimates of the people residing in Bosnia and Herzegovina think that over 500.000 people originating from Bosnia and Herzegovina nowadays live in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge if in the early days of the aggression against Croatia and vice versa? They went to Croatia, volunteers went to Croatia and then went back? And I mean volunteers from the ranks of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I know well about this, again there are assessments only, because there are no accurate figures. When the aggression of the Serbs, Montenegrins and so-called JNA against Croatia started, our estimates say that over 50.000 volunteers from Bosnia-Herzegovina went to defend the Republic of Croatia, that is their relatives, brothers and others, in the Republic of Croatia. In the same vein, some people, when the situation in Croatia calmed down, and when the war was activated in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is in late 1992, early 1993 and later, some men went back to Bosnia and Herzegovina to defend their homes, their hearths, their wives and children and so on and so forth. Our estimates speak of several tens of thousands of those who went back from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the attitude of Muslims, that is Bosniaks, to the organisation of the defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Could I have the interpretation so that we can follow? No, I don't have the text on the screen. I'd like to have the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Did you say the relations of -- between the Muslims or did you say the attitude to the defence? The French interpreter spoke about the relations. I'm asking whether your question was about the attitude of Muslims towards the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My exact question was, Your Honour, "what was the attitude of the Bosniaks, Muslims, towards the organisation of the defence, the organisation of the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean? " And we expect the witness to tell us something about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the early days of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the Croat Defence Council suffered the worst blows, suffered the brunt of the attack, both Croats and Muslims were in the HVO and an occasional Serb, too. That is, we defended -- we organised the defence together, but we felt, because that was the information we received from our commanders, that is we who were in the politics, received that kind of information, that the Muslims were engaged in tactical games when it came to the organisation of the defence. And later on, it was confirmed, because they had got ready to take us by surprise and betray us. When I say, "us," I mean the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We will come to that later on. We may belabour that point. Tell me, do you have any personal knowledge about the assistance lent to Bosniaks, Muslims: weapons, food, refugees?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Why, of course. After all, I am one of the principal men of the Croat people in that part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so in the beginning of the war in the -- towards the end of 1992 and in the beginning of 1993, the -- an overwhelming part of the assistance came from -- came by and large through Croatia and the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bender, but I must interrupt you. Your answers are -- we are getting your answers in the present tense. My colleague now warns me. When you said that you were one of the leading men, which period of time did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I thought that we had cleared it up, but I must warn you that the transcript reflects what you are saying, so I have to have this correction. I can hear your Croatian and my colleague is following it in English?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: All that I'm saying I'm saying about the time when the Croat community and Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna functioned. It was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you know we must correctly transconvey your words because the transcript said, "I am," that is that you are?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: No, I believe you understand what I'm saying. Let us avoid the misunderstandings, there should not be any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry for this interruption. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I said that we collected and distributed the humanitarian aid, armaments and the rest, that it went through Croatia and through the Croat community Herceg-Bosna, but we also had information that the Muslim side was also getting assistance and weapons through other channels too, from the Islamic world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. Now we move on to a different subject. That is the relations with the Bosniaks, Muslims, and my first question in this regard would be as follows. Could you describe to -- for the Honourable Court, or rather can you tell us what do you know about the relations between the Croats and the Muslims? And I'm referring to 1992 and 1993. But first let us --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Well, I said that in the early days of this war, and that is the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992, and for a large part of 1992, and even through part of 1993, Muslim -- Croats and Muslims were together. But in some areas, already as early as the end of 1992, and especially in the beginning of 1993, and in mid-1993, the Muslim side began to provoke incidents and killings of Croats, and as of May, 1993 onward, open attacks of the Muslim forces on Croats and the Croat lands. I know about incidents and murders of Croats in Konjic, Busovaca, in Mostar lands, and also this Honourable Court must know that in May and June, "Armija" of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is what they called them, that is the Muslim armed forces launched an open attack on the Croat Defence Council and the population of Mosta. Followed by the conquest of the north camp in Mostar, and in early July, 1993, it was also followed by the murder of -- or by the killing of 18 Croats, members of the Croat Defence Council, on the Dubrav Plateau which is the area between Stolic, Neum, Capljina and Mostar. Similar incidents also happened in other lands across Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, as a matter of fact, I was about to ask you, because we need to somehow get to this unfortunate 1993, or rather May of that year, I thought that perhaps you could explain to the Honourable Court a little bit about the relations which existed in 1992 and why did this conflict happen? Why did we now have these attacks? Why? Don't you think -- could you perhaps shed some light for the Honourable Court on these events? Of course about telling us only what you know. For instance, you mentioned Konjic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Well, yes. The Court ought to know, and I will explain why the early incidents happened and later on the open attack of the members of the Muslim armed forces, that is the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the Croat Defence Council. This was actually the struggle over territories, because the Serbs had already occupied a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, expelled Croats and especially the Bosniaks, because they were the majority, from East Bosnian lands, and those refugees came to this remnant of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when there are too many people in one area, then naturally there begins this struggle for that area, the struggle for survival, the "Lebensraum" and the Muslims must have thought that the lands which they had lost to the Serbs, that they could make up for them by taking over the lands where the Croats were the majority. And that is why these incidents and conflicts happened in Konjic and in Busovaca and later on in Rama, in Mostar, and so on and so forth. This is the struggle for space, the struggle for existence. And I must point out that we, in the politics, received information from our members of the Croat Defence Council that -- that the Muslims were piling up the humanitarian aid and weapons, getting ready for something, and we had -- and we also received information about some meetings between SDA representatives in Zenica -- of SDA representatives in Zenica, where they were getting ready to occupy the lands from Konjic downstream the Neretva, that is through Jablanica, Stolac, Capljina, and the most important thing, gaining access to the sea. Because, I believe the Honourable Court knows, there was a document about the plans of the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic about the foundation of an Islamic state, with the outlet to the sea and the outlet to the Sava. And I repeat, especially the access to the sea and the municipality of Neum have over 90 per cent of Croat population. And all -- and we knew about all those plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, what is the foundation for these claims? Because we heard testimonies here, and that is what international representatives were saying, that all the Croat officials, I do not know whether your name came up specifically, but the testimonies that we heard here in this courtroom, they all sang the same song we just heard, but that it was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, could Mr. Krsnik be a bit clear on what "song" we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you have to clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I used -- I did not mean a song, I meant everybody danced to the same tune. I did not mean a song sung, actually sung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used the words that Sir Martin Garrod used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't mean a real song either. I'd like to know what the question was to the witness about what policy and practice that all these international witnesses came in and according to Mr. Krsnik say. That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, we got a little bit confused by your question. I think you have to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters and the -- and Your Honours if I caused some confusion. At that time I used the same words that Sir Martin Garrod used and I don't remember anybody being taken aback by them. That is what he said, that is the Croat representatives always sang the same song, about the creation of an Islamic state and the Muslim outlet to the sea. Those were his words. And as I, fortunately or unfortunately, have a good memory, I simply used the same terminology. And asked this witness whether that was indeed so, or was there any foundation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must repeat to the Honourable Court what I already said, because I have sworn to tell the truth, and all that I'm saying is true. If the Honourable Court does not have certain documents which would corroborate my -- what I'm saying, I can supply them either for -- either to the counsel or to the Prosecutor or to the Court, and then you will be able to see that what I'm saying is the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender I was just about to ask you in fact what happened to all these documents and plans that you are aware of in the HVO? Where are they kept? Where have they been and what was the system of storing and cataloging and archiving such historical documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a lawyer and as a protagonist of the legislative function, I know well the laws which are in force and which regulate the matter. However, unfortunately, some of these documents have, by some channels unknown to me, reached the Prosecutor's Office, that is this Tribunal. We need to check therefore, that is somebody either made a mistake or misused his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Bender, that is not what Her Honour asked you. Her Honour asked you where was the documentation kept? Because we badly need authentic documents. For instance, where is the archive of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did I guess what you meant, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The archive of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the archive of the House of Representatives of the HDZ is kept in our lands. However, some of the documents unfortunately travelled by some other channels. Some of military documents and some others, I don't know which, but the HDZ documentation and the documentation of the legislative body is kept as prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And is it accessible to the Office of the Prosecutor or the Defence at any time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: Anyone who is interested to learn about it may get to see those documents in the prescribed, lawful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, you see, we once again have problems with the interpretation. Or I'm sorry, I know that we -- our interpreters are great, but maybe because you're too fast, it does not say - that is of our country and you finished. I know what you said but you have to say which country you meant.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: I always am referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina as my state and my homeland. That is quite clear. So nobody should draw any other conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But yes, we need to be cautious, you know, because somebody might draw a different conclusion if the meaning of what you said is misinterpreted. Because, you know, I am curious too, and I'm grateful to Judge Clark, but she encouraged me to ask you something which I didn't intend to ask you, but I will now. Who is the owner of documents which relate to the HVO and HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina yet are in Zagreb? We have come to call them here Zagreb archives or Zagreb evidence. Whose documentation is it? Who is its owner?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENDER
utterances.text: The owner of the documentation of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna and the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the Croat Defence Council is the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is Bosnia and Herzegovina. And these documents had to be kept in the archives in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know how did they get to Zagreb and did you ever, as representatives of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you ever go through this documentation? Do you have any idea what is called -- what is it that is called here the Zagreb archive? Has anyone informed you about that? Did you discuss it in the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think there are nine or ten questions in there. Could we possibly have one question at a time and not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And I'm still asking very basic questions to which we didn't get the answer. Surely, it's terribly important to you as defence council to be in possession of these remarkable documents which your witness -- your witness -- is telling us about and when I ask him about the documents, he goes on and answers something that has nothing to do with the question. Now, it's hard for you to cross-examine your own witness, so I'll ask him the questions, if you don't mind. Mr. Bender, you have said on a number of occasions that you in your position, as a very important person in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I think you said you were one of the vice-presidents, if not the vice-president to the Presidency, you said that, "We knew about plans," on a number of occasions. First of all, can I ask you what you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I talk about this plan and used word "we," we in the Croat community -- community Herceg-Bosna, we in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna and we in the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. By this, I mean the leadership of these institutions. The small circle of the leadership because we received information from our representatives and our agencies, let me put it quite bluntly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you receive information deriving from documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why, naturally. Every information must have some provenance, be it a document or a minutes or a note made at a meeting, during talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bender, for instance, if you say, "We saw plans for a Muslim attack and we were aware that the Muslims were storing humanitarian aid and weapons," what was the source of that particular information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, specifically concerning the information which has to do with the armaments and the stockpiling of armaments by the Muslims, the source of this information is conversations with our commanders in the Croat Defence Council, who had noticed that all the weapons and ammunition distributed to the Muslims and Croats to fight the Serbs, was not being used, that part of the humanitarian relief was not being distributed amongst the soldiers, but stored somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, sir, about the contents of your information. I'm asking you about the source. Specifically, you said that, "We had all those plans." And you referred to various places. Do you mean you had documents or were you talking about conversations which you had with people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said some documents specifically -- well, for instance, referred to this meeting in Zenica, about the preparation of the aggression against the Neretva valley. There is a document and it can be made available to the Honourable Court. There are documents which confirm murders in the territories of Konjic and Busovaca, there are also relevant police authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm talking about plans, not events or incidents. I'm talking about plans, because you gave very specific evidence about plans and documents which you had, and then I said, you know, and in fact, Mr. Krsnik said, "the defence might like to have those documents," and indeed, I don't blame him for that. But I would ask you, Mr. Bender, what was the system that was utilised in the HVO for receiving documents, storing them, cataloging them, and archiving them? I asked you that ten minutes ago. And perhaps, as it's 7.00, and we have certain arrangements with the interpreters that they finish at 7.00, we can deal with it tomorrow morning. And you'll be able to think about the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I have to warn you, as I did other witnesses, that during your stay in The Hague, you are still under the oath, so do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. No problem. I'll be in my hotel room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
